# Sahaj Solar Limited | SME research | Master Prompt v3.0

Information available through **20 October 2026**; market inputs through the **19 October 2026 NSE close**. Retrieved 24 October 2026. Amounts are ₹ crore unless stated. Position 348 in the SME universe. This is research, not an execution instruction or an allocation recommendation.

## 1. Executive Verdict

**Hold — unresolved.** Sahaj combines solar modules, government-linked pumping and EPC execution with reported rapid expansion, but earnings have not become dependable cash: FY26 consolidated revenue was ₹419.1935 crore, owners' PAT ₹29.5727 crore and reported CFO **negative ₹78.2985 crore**. Debt, receivables, retention and unverified cash restrictions matter more than the apparently low earnings multiple. Primary borrowing notes disclose multiple financing against the same receivables/inventories, while the auditor reports an unmodified opinion, effective IFC and no default. These facts must coexist, not be converted into an allegation of fraud or an assertion of safety. The September noncooperating/negative credit-rating transition, subsequent lender-NOC withdrawal and management's reported April ₹100 crore repayment are all retained. This is a **working-capital-intensive execution/collection-repair thesis**, not an evidence-backed compounder. Resolution requires reconciled lender security and cash-flow records, demonstrable collections, available liquidity and funded capex, not merely a lower share price. [E01–E08]

## 4. Business Overview

The business manufactures PV modules and supplies/installs solar pumping and EPC systems. Customer economics combine equipment cost, tender qualification, execution, warranty/service and collection from government-linked projects. It is not an integrated cell/wafer manufacturer or an already operating 1.8 GWh battery producer. Revenue recognition, receivables and retention can precede cash for long periods; orders and receivable-linked supplier arrangements are not cash receipts. The original group perimeter changed across years, including domestic subsidiaries and new overseas entities, so group growth is not automatically organic. [E09–E12]

Integrated solar-system supplier and project executor with in-house PV module assembly and group manufacturing of structures and controllers. Solar water pumping systems, off-grid/rooftop/ground-mounted EPC and maintenance dominate the disclosed historical mix; this is not a pure module-manufacturing exposure.

Tender qualification, procurement, assembly, installation, inspection and customer acceptance generate revenue; government collection and supplier-credit timing govern cash. Five-year warranty/maintenance obligations create continuing cost and execution exposure, not necessarily high-margin recurring revenue.

FY24 product mix was approximately70.49% pumps and27.11% modules; domestic revenue99.22%, export/deemed export0.78%. These are dated IPO-period observations, not FY26 mix. Top10customer share was67.42% inFY24; the FY25 primary rating reported top5customers73%. Top10supplier purchases85.4879crore represented42.38% of revenue, not42.38% of procurement. Supplier-concentration denominators are not interchanged. [prospectus, rating_sep25]

Domestic module expansion: Management said domestic 1.5 GW project put on hold in Jan–Feb 2026. No evidence of full commissioning by cutoff. [rating_sep25, call_may26]

750 MW UAE module venture: SHA and legal incorporation milestones achieved; additional June capital infusion announced, not established as paid. Plant commissioning, utilization, project finance and commercial output ND. [call_may26, sha_uae_may26, uae_incorporation_jun26, uae_capital_jun26]

1.8 GWh BESS, Dakor: Board approved, not commissioned; no BESS orders, utilization, unit margin or working-capital cycle disclosed. [bess_oct19]

Recycling: May 2026 management says facility commissioned and EPR certification awaited. Verified throughput, certification and revenue ND. [call_may26]

Mauritius subsidiary: Incorporated Feb 11; Oct 6 MUR 10,000 subscription completed, 100% owned; Oct 7 filing says business not commenced. [mauritius_oct26]

The May 2026 call identifies approximately ₹60 crore of receivables linked to supplier payments. That may reduce the immediate net funding burden, but the balance sheet already includes those payables. They are not netted out of receivables and then credited again as a separate financing inflow. Contracts, ageing and enforceability of the linkage remain material. Government exposure reduces neither payment-delay risk nor capital intensity to zero. [E07, E09]

## 5. Moat / Industry Position

| Proposed advantage | Mechanism and supporting evidence | Durability / failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| Integrated module/pump/EPC execution | Qualification, procurement, service and execution experience help win and fulfill tenders | Contestable by qualified suppliers; no verified enduring pricing premium, switching cost or upstream cost advantage |
| Customer/project experience | Actual expansion and a disclosed backlog support commercial access | Government payment timing, rebidding and performance obligations can overwhelm thin cash economics |
| Domestic module manufacturing | Existing 100 MW facility provides a manufacturing capability | Purchased cells/input exposure and much larger competitors limit structural cost claims; certifications do not prove excess returns |
| New BESS/recycling/offshore options | Board approval, prototype/certification and proposed capacity can open products | Not current revenue capacity; commissioning, EPR/customer qualification, utilization and financing remain separate gates |

No defensible market-share denominator or verified niche-leadership percentage was located. Capacity is not production, output is not external sales, and backlog is not a moat. May management descriptions of utilization conflict: one speaker cites about 60%, another 30–35 MW of one-shift own-consumption production. Neither is silently selected as the verified annual utilization. [E09–E12]

Primary economic comparators are selected for solar modules, pumping and EPC/working-capital economics rather than similar market capitalization alone:

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shakti Pumps (India) Limited | FY26 / Consolidated, integrated pumps/motors/controllers with solar agricultural pumping, exports and electric pumps; larger manufacturing and service footprint than Sahaj. | 2697.60 | 15.63% | 0.48x | peer_shakti |
| Solex Energy Limited | FY26 / Issuer FY26 financial presentation, PV modules plus EPC; 4 GW module manufacturing capacity claimed as achieved, not the future 10 GW vision. | 1618.06 | 11.35% | 2.04x | peer_solex |

**Shakti Pumps (India) Limited:** FY26 solar-pump installations grew 20% to 86,086 per management, yet EBITDA margin fell from 24.0% to 15.6%. Issuer attributes pressure to lower Magel Tyala realization and increased raw-material/logistics costs. This directly challenges a broad solar-pump pricing-power thesis. Positive CFO is less than half PAT; receivables and working-capital loans remain substantial. Cash flow and cash balances are presentation-rounded; no unrestricted-cash/net debt conclusion without full notes. Own pump technology and much larger manufacturing/service/export footprint; Sahaj buys pumps and has a different EPC mix. Presentation EBITDA excludes other income, confirmed by PBT/finance/depreciation bridge within rounding. No full lease/covenant audit performed.

**Solex Energy Limited:** Sales grew 144.3%, but normalized margin declined from 11.63% to 11.35%. Large module scale does not automatically produce better margins than the integrated project mix. CFO exceeded PAT, but trade payables increased ₹366.7 cr while receivables increased ₹242.2 cr. Supplier financing materially affects the cash outcome. Reported ROCE/ROE lack matched normalization here; do not compare reported return labels directly to Sahaj average-capital calculations. Module-heavy mix, different scale and capacity ramp. Reported EBITDA includes other income; subtract 3.07 cr for comparable operating numerator. Cash and bank balances combined include potentially restricted amounts; leases may reside outside presentation borrowing captions.

**Alpex Solar Limited:** Sales grew 185%, but normalized operating margin fell from 16.06% to 14.38%; higher volume and capacity do not establish price-setting power. Inventory/receivable/other-current-asset investment pushed CFO negative. Borrowings plus leases approximately ₹536.52 cr and substantial capex make funding and utilization central. Other bank balances are not assumed unrestricted cash. The business is not treated as net-debt-free. Faster manufacturing ramp and different product/order mix; reporting uses Ind AS, while Sahaj financials have accounting differences. Corrected audited CF headings distinguish FY25 comparative from erroneously printed FY24 in original filing. BS debt/lease numbers checked against original PDF image.

Peer data are dated operating benchmarks, not synchronized price targets. Consolidated versus standalone scope, different reporting periods, accounting policies, integration and subsidy exposure are stated. A one-year peer CFO/PAT is not presented as comparable to Sahaj's multiyear ratio. No peer-average factor is used to fill a missing Sahaj factor. [E13]

Latest comparable half-year (H2 FY26, ending31March2026) revenue 308.07 versus 231.67 grew 32.98%; owners PAT grew 7.02%. Bonus-restated EPS11.13 versus11.28 did not improve. H2 supplied 73.49% of FY26 sales, so it must not be doubled into a forecast. No H1 FY27 results or standalone half-year CFO were invented. [F_R26 PDF18]

Reported growth is not defensibly labeled wholly organic or volume-driven. FY26 pump installations and order mix establish activity but do not decompose revenue. Domestic new ventures, an overseas subsidiary and new joint ventures complicate scope; no acquired-revenue bridge was verified. The FY26 management-reported >8,000 pump installations is an annual unit indicator, but a matching FY25 unit/horsepower/price series is not verified.

The preferred five-year window cannot be described as comparable organic growth merely because six revenue numbers can be assembled. FY22 lacked a holding–subsidiary relationship at its year-end, and the restatement itself says group composition differs across years. Parent growth is an additional cross-check, not a substitute for eliminating intercompany sales or separating price, volume and project mix. Ten-year and TTM measures without adequate comparable observations remain ND. Recent profit growth and a cheap P/E do not justify a revenue-score upgrade. [E01, E02, E10]

Revenue quality requires a bridge from module volumes/realizations, EPC execution, new entities and acquisitions to external net revenue. A rising absolute sales base is real commercial progress, but neither the solar TAM nor BESS capacity earns a REV point. A 30% management FY27 target is recorded as a statement, not copied into the supported base case. [E09–E12]

## 7. Growth Quality & Reinvestment Runway

The disclosed March 2026 backlog of about ₹402 crore comprises roughly ₹107 crore solar pumps, ₹44 crore off-grid and ₹251 crore grid-connected work. Execution windows span 3–18 months, so management's expectation of completion during FY27 requires delivery and collections, not automatic conversion on day one. The 10,000 bulk-milk-cooler partnership opportunity was a proof-of-concept/anticipated-order initiative, **not in that backlog**. Tender bids and nonbinding pipeline are not sales. [E09]

The October 19 board approved a **1.8 GWh BESS facility, approximately ₹25 crore excluding already constructed premises, proposed financing through debt/internal accruals, within 12 months**; current BESS capacity and utilization were NIL. The model spends ₹25 crore in staged cash and does not create free revenue from the announcement. Existing PPE, CWIP and capital advances remain committed capital; transferring them into PPE is not a cash inflow or a second capex payment. Domestic module expansion had been placed on hold, UAE capacity was not yet installed and the recycler was awaiting EPR certification according to May commentary. [E11, E12]

| Scaling layer | Model treatment | Evidence limit |
|---|---|---|
| Existing EPC/module mix | ₹420 crore pre-entry annual pace; post-entry growth 2%/12%/20% with shock/margin differences | Analyst scenarios, not backlog-derived guaranteed invoices |
| Current and new manufacturing | Existing capital plus 25 BESS cash, qualification lags and incremental fixed investment | ₹420 crore sales envelope is analytical, not an asserted physical plant ceiling |
| Working capital | Receivables including retention, inventories, supplier advances, accruals and collateral all move with operations | Receivable/supplier matching and escrow availability need reconciliation |
| Terminal growth | 2%/3% with explicit fixed assets, ONWC, collateral and operating-reserve reinvestment | No perpetual growth without the cash and capital it consumes |

Growth can increase enterprise revenue while destroying per-share value if collection delays force repeated issues. The finite financing panels therefore charge fees/interest, enforce whole-share issues and authorization limits, retain unsuccessful trials and never turn a negative cash balance into an invented unlimited loan. GQS remains constrained by persistent cash weakness and the stated evidence gaps. [E04, E07, E14]

## 8. Management, Governance & Execution

The strongest reliability concern is an explicit FY2026 borrowing-note disclosure, not an inferred allegation: some receivables and inventory were offered to more than one lender, producing multiple financing of the same assets, and management says allocation is being reconciled and regularized. No lender-confirmed cure was located. Counterevidence must remain visible: Mistry & Shah issued an unmodified opinion and effective-IFC opinion; CARO reports no loan default or fraud and says term loans were applied for their purpose. These findings support an unresolved research hold, not a claim of proven diversion, intentional fraud or actual insolvency. [F_AR26 pp79–92,108–111,141–148]

This follows recurring bank-reporting differences. FY2025 CARO Annexure C shows debtor differences of ₹58.50 crore in May 2024 and ₹50.8279 crore in March 2025. The company cites IREDA-funded debtors and provisional unaudited figures, although the table direction and prose are not fully reconciled. FY2026 note38 shows quarterly differences of +₹11.1356 crore, −₹4.4968 crore, +₹27.8237 crore and −₹10.1531 crore and attributes them to late retention entries and supplier/raw-material scope. Legitimate collateral eligibility can explain differences; only a facility-level, lender-confirmed reconciliation can establish that this explanation resolves the current multiple-financing issue. [F_AR25 PDF111; F_AR26 pp92,137]

Original audit opinions for FY2021–FY2026 were examined instead of treating an IPO restatement as six fresh statutory audits. Rohan Thakkar resigned in September 2023 and Mistry & Shah succeeded it; B.V. Zalawadia performed the earlier IPO restatement on which Mistry relied. The resignation reason is not independently established, so neither mandatory rotation nor an information-withholding dispute is asserted. Audit-trail software is affirmed in FY2024–FY2026. Clean opinions and available original records support basic reported-history analysis, but do not repair the old cash-flow classification and group-comparability gaps. [F_AR21–F_AR26; F_IPO pp3–6,44–46] For FY2022 specifically, p20 refers to an enclosed IFC opinion, whereas p17 disclaims an effectiveness opinion and the reviewed pp15–31 do not show a separate conclusion. This conflicting enclosure reference is retained; the separate IFC conclusion remains ND, not adverse. [F_AR22 PDF17,20]

Governance is mixed rather than demonstrably abusive. FY2025 secretarial exceptions identify delayed/missing UPSI database entries and earnings-call/presentation filings despite the board summary saying no qualifications. FY2026 contains five similar procedural observations, with management responses promising better timing. Related-party disclosures show ₹1.9356 crore advanced to common-control Veracity Recycler and a ₹1.6957 crore closing balance, while rent to the MD rose from ₹0.0780 crore to ₹1.0324 crore. The MD also received ₹0.2749 crore salary; Veracity Recycler interest was ₹0.0565 crore. These deserve terms, recovery and rent-benchmark checks during heavy cash burn. Parent loans to VEIPL of ₹4.9849 crore and VREPL of ₹0.4150 crore are eliminated within the consolidated group and should not be confused with external common-control exposure. Conversely, the auditor describes loan terms as not prejudicial, reports regular repayment and no amounts over 90 days; management discloses the transactions as arm’s length, and the MD also supplied ₹1.0350 crore net funding. Commercial RPTs alone are not proof of cash leakage. [F_AR25 PDF80; F_AR26 pp47–49,85,132–136]

The ₹64.3356 crore of MSME payables more than one year past due is an economic obligation, not just a presentation footnote. Earlier disclosure of incomplete MSME classification and omitted interest provisioning limits historical comparability. Collection-linked supplier arrangements and a fall in overall payables are relevant counterevidence, but cannot be assumed to waive overdue amounts or eliminate statutory exposure. It is necessary to verify settlement terms, payments and any interest/penalty treatment before relying on suppliers to finance further growth. [F_AR23 PDF141–142; F_AR26 pp165–166]

The IPO allocation is not a stand-alone governance failure. The disclosed employee discount explains the difference between nominal ₹52.56 crore and actual ₹52.524 crore proceeds, and the company reports full utilization by FY2025. The proposed subsequent preferential/share swap was withdrawn rather than completed. These resolved facts should not be recycled as unexplained dilution or missing-proceeds allegations. The remaining question is economic: whether working-capital deployment and the new factory produce cash returns without another unfavorable financing cycle. [F_PROS cover; F_IPOUTIL pp1–3; F_AR25 pp62–63; F_AR26 pp35–36,160–162]

Audit-control evidence is period-specific. FY2021 contains a separate adequate/effective IFC opinion as at 31 March 2021, dated 10 January 2022 (PDF61–64). Its CARO annexure explicitly reports no default/fraud or term-loan misuse while noting PF, ESI and GST deposit delays (PDF66). FY2022 has the conflicting enclosure reference and responsibility disclaimer described above; its separate conclusion remains ND. A separate adequate/effective IFC opinion is present for FY2023, and FY2024–FY2026 also report effective controls. For audit trails, FY2023 says the software requirement applies from 1 April 2023; FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 affirm audit-trail software. No adverse trail qualification was located, but that wording is not proof that every historical edit log was independently tested. The Ind AS language in FY2025 audit boilerplate is not evidence of a transition when the actual policies and statements use the AS basis. [F_AR21–F_AR26; annual audit register]

The decisive unresolved matter is not an inferred allegation: original FY26 borrowing notes explicitly describe certain receivables/inventories offered as security to more than one lender and the resulting multiple financing, with management reconciling and regularizing allocation. Quarterly bank-statement differences require examination alongside this note. The fair counterweight is the audit's unmodified opinion, effective IFC conclusion and no reported default, not an assumption that the note is immaterial. Resolution requires lender-wise assets, priority/security documentation, acknowledged drawing-power reconciliation and the resulting borrowing/cash positions. [E03, E04]

The rating chronology must be read in order: BBB-/Stable/A3 in September 2025; BBB-(INC)/Negative/A3(INC) communicated September 10, 2026; then withdrawal at the company's request after lender NOC. The company did not request the adverse revision itself. Withdrawal is not proof of repayment, restored Stable outlook or a new live rating. Conversely, noncooperation is not itself a payment default. [E08]

The strongest credible failure chain is government/project collections slip → high retention and aged debtors remain → suppliers withdraw payment linkage or lenders restrict overlapping collateral → borrowing cost/available limits worsen → BESS and EPC require cash before receipts → discounted equity or asset sales impair existing owners. Capex delay then reduces growth while fixed costs and warranty commitments persist. A quoted drawdown alone is not impairment; an unfinanceable earning asset base or dilutive recapitalization can be. [E03, E04, E07–E12]

The single thesis-break variable is **collectible, unrestricted operating cash after lender and supplier claims**, not headline PAT. The strongest contrary evidence to a purely pessimistic view is actual revenue execution, profitable operating results, no auditor-reported default, management-stated early debt repayment, reported supplier linkage and sufficient conditional collection-repair paths to demonstrate that cash improvement could materially change economics. Those positives must be verified rather than dismissed. Impairment risk is High because cash/claim uncertainty and security overlap combine; this is not a quantified fraud probability. Failed scenario values are NS rather than ordinary shareholder prices. [E01–E14]

The tests distinguish revenue growth, enterprise value, common equity, fully diluted shares and price return. Five-year 5× needs 37.97% annual price appreciation and 10× needs 58.49%; over ten years the requirements are 17.46% and 25.89%. Dividend-free total-return tests further include modeled trading friction. The common identity is revenue multiple × owner-margin multiple × old/new diluted shares × terminal/current P/E where positive normalized earnings make it meaningful; model outputs instead use an enterprise-to-equity bridge with debt, retained claims, NCI and reserves. The feasible fast-collection tests are **Speculative / unsupported**, not evidence-backed multibagger targets. They require collection repair, sustained margins, financing access, execution beyond the current order base and material reinvestment. Every trial reports terminal revenue, incremental capital and whole-share dilution; a lower 8× EBIT valuation is included. No unsupported accessible-market share is invented, and no precise probability is assigned. A module-capacity or GWh headline alone cannot support the required revenue. [E09–E14]

## 14. Final Classification & Conditional Action

**Hold — unresolved; research priority, not eligible for a favorable investment conclusion.** The numerical matrix is not applied to an NS score as though it were a low number. The compounder designation fails the evidence/gate requirements and does not follow from a low P/E, solar demand or rapid historical group revenue growth. Price alone cannot clear financial-reliability, funding and organic-growth questions. [E01–E15]

For an existing holder this record identifies cash, funding, reliability and execution risks to investigate; it does not assert a portfolio exit count without holdings, tax and execution context. New evidence could produce scoreable factors and a new classification. The exact three scores are preserved separately; no undisclosed overall blend or invented universe rank is supplied. sections.title: Executive Verdict
sections.content_markdown: **Hold — unresolved.** Sahaj combines solar modules, government-linked pumping and EPC execution with reported rapid expansion, but earnings have not become dependable cash: FY26 consolidated revenue was ₹419.1935 crore, owners' PAT ₹29.5727 crore and reported CFO **negative ₹78.2985 crore**. Debt, receivables, retention and unverified cash restrictions matter more than the apparently low earnings multiple. Primary borrowing notes disclose multiple financing against the same receivables/inventories, while the auditor reports an unmodified opinion, effective IFC and no default. These facts must coexist, not be converted into an allegation of fraud or an assertion of safety. The September noncooperating/negative credit-rating transition, subsequent lender-NOC withdrawal and management's reported April ₹100 crore repayment are all retained. This is a **working-capital-intensive execution/collection-repair thesis**, not an evidence-backed compounder. Resolution requires reconciled lender security and cash-flow records, demonstrable collections, available liquidity and funded capex, not merely a lower share price. [E01–E08]

Every factor is assigned once. BQS weights are GOV 20%, MOAT 20%, REV 12%, DUR 10%, CAP 12%, CASH 10%, BAL 8%, EXEC 8%. GQS weights are REV 40%, DUR 20%, EARN 15%, CAP 15%, CASH 10%. IAS is 25% of final BQS plus R 35%, D 20%, P 10%, L 10%; GQS is not added again. Exact Decimal arithmetic, original weights and conventional half-up one-decimal display are retained. Missing-data bounds are mathematical bounds, **not confidence intervals**; no midpoint, neutral score or reweighting is substituted for NS.

BQS: GOV=0.8000, MOAT=0.8000, REV=NS, DUR=0.5000, CAP=NS, CASH=0.2000, BAL=0.2400, EXEC=0.3200. Known contribution=2.8600.

GQS: REV=NS, DUR=1.0000, EARN=0.7500, CAP=NS, CASH=0.2000. Known contribution=1.9500.

IAS: Q=NS, R=NS, D=0.6000, P=NS, L=0.3000. Known contribution=0.9000. IAS quality-propagated mathematical bound: 2.1250–6.7150.

Persistent poor cash realization triggers the disclosed **GQS ceiling of 5**, but never replaces NS with 5. There is no governance/funding numeric override based solely on a model shortfall, noncooperating rating or a disclosed security reconciliation. Historical scores above 8 are not assigned without an appropriate reliable cycle. The two uncertain scored judgments and their ±1 changes are in scores.json; they do not override the binding holds. [E01–E15]

sections.title: Business Overview
sections.content_markdown:
The business manufactures PV modules and supplies/installs solar pumping and EPC systems. Customer economics combine equipment cost, tender qualification, execution, warranty/service and collection from government-linked projects. It is not an integrated cell/wafer manufacturer or an already operating 1.8 GWh battery producer. Revenue recognition, receivables and retention can precede cash for long periods; orders and receivable-linked supplier arrangements are not cash receipts. The original group perimeter changed across years, including domestic subsidiaries and new overseas entities, so group growth is not automatically organic. [E09–E12]

Integrated solar-system supplier and project executor with in-house PV module assembly and group manufacturing of structures and controllers. Solar water pumping systems, off-grid/rooftop/ground-mounted EPC and maintenance dominate the disclosed historical mix; this is not a pure module-manufacturing exposure.

Tender qualification, procurement, assembly, installation, inspection and customer acceptance generate revenue; government collection and supplier-credit timing govern cash. Five-year warranty/maintenance obligations create continuing cost and execution exposure, not necessarily high-margin recurring revenue.

FY24 product mix was approximately70.49% pumps and27.11% modules; domestic revenue99.22%, export/deemed export0.78%. These are dated IPO-period observations, not FY26 mix. Top10customer share was67.42% inFY24; the FY25 primary rating reported top5customers73%. Top10supplier purchases85.4879crore represented42.38% of revenue, not42.38% of procurement. Supplier-concentration denominators are not interchanged. [prospectus, rating_sep25]

Domestic module expansion: Management said domestic 1.5 GW project put on hold in Jan–Feb 2026. No evidence of full commissioning by cutoff. [rating_sep25, call_may26]

750 MW UAE module venture: SHA and legal incorporation milestones achieved; additional June capital infusion announced, not established as paid. Plant commissioning, utilization, project finance and commercial output ND. [call_may26, sha_uae_may26, uae_incorporation_jun26, uae_capital_jun26]

1.8 GWh BESS, Dakor: Board approved, not commissioned; no BESS orders, utilization, unit margin or working-capital cycle disclosed. [bess_oct19]

Recycling: May 2026 management says facility commissioned and EPR certification awaited. Verified throughput, certification and revenue ND. [call_may26]

Mauritius subsidiary: Incorporated Feb 11; Oct 6 MUR 10,000 subscription completed, 100% owned; Oct 7 filing says business not commenced. [mauritius_oct26]

The May 2026 call identifies approximately ₹60 crore of receivables linked to supplier payments. That may reduce the immediate net funding burden, but the balance sheet already includes those payables. They are not netted out of receivables and then credited again as a separate financing inflow. Contracts, ageing and enforceability of the linkage remain material. Government exposure reduces neither payment-delay risk nor capital intensity to zero. [E07, E09]

| Proposed advantage | Mechanism and supporting evidence | Durability / failure mode |

| Integrated module/pump/EPC execution | Qualification, procurement, service and execution experience help win and fulfill tenders | Contestable by qualified suppliers; no verified enduring pricing premium, switching cost or upstream cost advantage |
| Customer/project experience | Actual expansion and a disclosed backlog support commercial access | Government payment timing, rebidding and performance obligations can overwhelm thin cash economics |
| Domestic module manufacturing | Existing 100 MW facility provides a manufacturing capability | Purchased cells/input exposure and much larger competitors limit structural cost claims; certifications do not prove excess returns |
| New BESS/recycling/offshore options | Board approval, prototype/certification and proposed capacity can open products | Not current revenue capacity; commissioning, EPR/customer qualification, utilization and financing remain separate gates |

No defensible market-share denominator or verified niche-leadership percentage was located. Capacity is not production, output is not external sales, and backlog is not a moat. May management descriptions of utilization conflict: one speaker cites about 60%, another 30–35 MW of one-shift own-consumption production. Neither is silently selected as the verified annual utilization. [E09–E12]

Primary economic comparators are selected for solar modules, pumping and EPC/working-capital economics rather than similar market capitalization alone:

| Shakti Pumps (India) Limited | FY26 / Consolidated, integrated pumps/motors/controllers with solar agricultural pumping, exports and electric pumps; larger manufacturing and service footprint than Sahaj. | 2697.60 | 15.63% | 0.48x | peer_shakti |

| Alpex Solar Limited | FY26 / Consolidated FY26 audited results with June 1 corrigendum; module manufacturing, solar pumps and EPC, with rapid module/cell capacity investment. | 2223.27 | 14.38% | -0.57x | peer_alpex, peer_alpex_results |

**Shakti Pumps (India) Limited:** FY26 solar-pump installations grew 20% to 86,086 per management, yet EBITDA margin fell from 24.0% to 15.6%. Issuer attributes pressure to lower Magel Tyala realization and increased raw-material/logistics costs. This directly challenges a broad solar-pump pricing-power thesis. Positive CFO is less than half PAT; receivables and working-capital loans remain substantial. Cash flow and cash balances are presentation-rounded; no unrestricted-cash/net debt conclusion without full notes. Own pump technology and much larger manufacturing/service/export footprint; Sahaj buys pumps and has a different EPC mix. Presentation EBITDA excludes other income, confirmed by PBT/finance/depreciation bridge within rounding. No full lease/covenant audit performed.

**Solex Energy Limited:** Sales grew 144.3%, but normalized margin declined from 11.63% to 11.35%. Large module scale does not automatically produce better margins than the integrated project mix. CFO exceeded PAT, but trade payables increased ₹366.7 cr while receivables increased ₹242.2 cr. Supplier financing materially affects the cash outcome. Reported ROCE/ROE lack matched normalization here; do not compare reported return labels directly to Sahaj average-capital calculations. Module-heavy mix, different scale and capacity ramp. Reported EBITDA includes other income; subtract 3.07 cr for comparable operating numerator. Cash and bank balances combined include potentially restricted amounts; leases may reside outside presentation borrowing captions.

**Alpex Solar Limited:** Sales grew 185%, but normalized operating margin fell from 16.06% to 14.38%; higher volume and capacity do not establish price-setting power. Inventory/receivable/other-current-asset investment pushed CFO negative. Borrowings plus leases approximately ₹536.52 cr and substantial capex make funding and utilization central. Other bank balances are not assumed unrestricted cash. The business is not treated as net-debt-free. Faster manufacturing ramp and different product/order mix; reporting uses Ind AS, while Sahaj financials have accounting differences. Corrected audited CF headings distinguish FY25 comparative from erroneously printed FY24 in original filing. BS debt/lease numbers checked against original PDF image.

Peer data are dated operating benchmarks, not synchronized price targets. Consolidated versus standalone scope, different reporting periods, accounting policies, integration and subsidy exposure are stated. A one-year peer CFO/PAT is not presented as comparable to Sahaj's multiyear ratio. No peer-average factor is used to fill a missing Sahaj factor. [E13]

sections.title: Growth Quality & Reinvestment Runway
sections.content_markdown:
The disclosed March 2026 backlog of about ₹402 crore comprises roughly ₹107 crore solar pumps, ₹44 crore off-grid and ₹251 crore grid-connected work. Execution windows span 3–18 months, so management's expectation of completion during FY27 requires delivery and collections, not automatic conversion on day one. The 10,000 bulk-milk-cooler partnership opportunity was a proof-of-concept/anticipated-order initiative, **not in that backlog**. Tender bids and nonbinding pipeline are not sales. [E09]

The October 19 board approved a **1.8 GWh BESS facility, approximately ₹25 crore excluding already constructed premises, proposed financing through debt/internal accruals, within 12 months**; current BESS capacity and utilization were NIL. The model spends ₹25 crore in staged cash and does not create free revenue from the announcement. Existing PPE, CWIP and capital advances remain committed capital; transferring them into PPE is not a cash inflow or a second capex payment. Domestic module expansion had been placed on hold, UAE capacity was not yet installed and the recycler was awaiting EPR certification according to May commentary. [E11, E12]

| Scaling layer | Model treatment | Evidence limit |
|---|---|---|
| Existing EPC/module mix | ₹420 crore pre-entry annual pace; post-entry growth 2%/12%/20% with shock/margin differences | Analyst scenarios, not backlog-derived guaranteed invoices |
| Current and new manufacturing | Existing capital plus 25 BESS cash, qualification lags and incremental fixed investment | ₹420 crore sales envelope is analytical, not an asserted physical plant ceiling |
| Working capital | Receivables including retention, inventories, supplier advances, accruals and collateral all move with operations | Receivable/supplier matching and escrow availability need reconciliation |
| Terminal growth | 2%/3% with explicit fixed assets, ONWC, collateral and operating-reserve reinvestment | No perpetual growth without the cash and capital it consumes |

Growth can increase enterprise revenue while destroying per-share value if collection delays force repeated issues. The finite financing panels therefore charge fees/interest, enforce whole-share issues and authorization limits, retain unsuccessful trials and never turn a negative cash balance into an invented unlimited loan. GQS remains constrained by persistent cash weakness and the stated evidence gaps. [E04, E07, E14]

sections.title: Management, Governance & Execution
sections.content_markdown:
The strongest reliability concern is an explicit FY2026 borrowing-note disclosure, not an inferred allegation: some receivables and inventory were offered to more than one lender, producing multiple financing of the same assets, and management says allocation is being reconciled and regularized. No lender-confirmed cure was located. Counterevidence must remain visible: Mistry & Shah issued an unmodified opinion and effective-IFC opinion; CARO reports no loan default or fraud and says term loans were applied for their purpose. These findings support an unresolved research hold, not a claim of proven diversion, intentional fraud or actual insolvency. [F_AR26 pp79–92,108–111,141–148]

This follows recurring bank-reporting differences. FY2025 CARO Annexure C shows debtor differences of ₹58.50 crore in May 2024 and ₹50.8279 crore in March 2025. The company cites IREDA-funded debtors and provisional unaudited figures, although the table direction and prose are not fully reconciled. FY2026 note38 shows quarterly differences of +₹11.1356 crore, −₹4.4968 crore, +₹27.8237 crore and −₹10.1531 crore and attributes them to late retention entries and supplier/raw-material scope. Legitimate collateral eligibility can explain differences; only a facility-level, lender-confirmed reconciliation can establish that this explanation resolves the current multiple-financing issue. [F_AR25 PDF111; F_AR26 pp92,137]

Original audit opinions for FY2021–FY2026 were examined instead of treating an IPO restatement as six fresh statutory audits. Rohan Thakkar resigned in September 2023 and Mistry & Shah succeeded it; B.V. Zalawadia performed the earlier IPO restatement on which Mistry relied. The resignation reason is not independently established, so neither mandatory rotation nor an information-withholding dispute is asserted. Audit-trail software is affirmed in FY2024–FY2026. Clean opinions and available original records support basic reported-history analysis, but do not repair the old cash-flow classification and group-comparability gaps. [F_AR21–F_AR26; F_IPO pp3–6,44–46] For FY2022 specifically, p20 refers to an enclosed IFC opinion, whereas p17 disclaims an effectiveness opinion and the reviewed pp15–31 do not show a separate conclusion. This conflicting enclosure reference is retained; the separate IFC conclusion remains ND, not adverse. [F_AR22 PDF17,20]

Governance is mixed rather than demonstrably abusive. FY2025 secretarial exceptions identify delayed/missing UPSI database entries and earnings-call/presentation filings despite the board summary saying no qualifications. FY2026 contains five similar procedural observations, with management responses promising better timing. Related-party disclosures show ₹1.9356 crore advanced to common-control Veracity Recycler and a ₹1.6957 crore closing balance, while rent to the MD rose from ₹0.0780 crore to ₹1.0324 crore. The MD also received ₹0.2749 crore salary; Veracity Recycler interest was ₹0.0565 crore. These deserve terms, recovery and rent-benchmark checks during heavy cash burn. Parent loans to VEIPL of ₹4.9849 crore and VREPL of ₹0.4150 crore are eliminated within the consolidated group and should not be confused with external common-control exposure. Conversely, the auditor describes loan terms as not prejudicial, reports regular repayment and no amounts over 90 days; management discloses the transactions as arm’s length, and the MD also supplied ₹1.0350 crore net funding. Commercial RPTs alone are not proof of cash leakage. [F_AR25 PDF80; F_AR26 pp47–49,85,132–136]

The ₹64.3356 crore of MSME payables more than one year past due is an economic obligation, not just a presentation footnote. Earlier disclosure of incomplete MSME classification and omitted interest provisioning limits historical comparability. Collection-linked supplier arrangements and a fall in overall payables are relevant counterevidence, but cannot be assumed to waive overdue amounts or eliminate statutory exposure. It is necessary to verify settlement terms, payments and any interest/penalty treatment before relying on suppliers to finance further growth. [F_AR23 PDF141–142; F_AR26 pp165–166]

The IPO allocation is not a stand-alone governance failure. The disclosed employee discount explains the difference between nominal ₹52.56 crore and actual ₹52.524 crore proceeds, and the company reports full utilization by FY2025. The proposed subsequent preferential/share swap was withdrawn rather than completed. These resolved facts should not be recycled as unexplained dilution or missing-proceeds allegations. The remaining question is economic: whether working-capital deployment and the new factory produce cash returns without another unfavorable financing cycle. [F_PROS cover; F_IPOUTIL pp1–3; F_AR25 pp62–63; F_AR26 pp35–36,160–162]

Audit-control evidence is period-specific. FY2021 contains a separate adequate/effective IFC opinion as at 31 March 2021, dated 10 January 2022 (PDF61–64). Its CARO annexure explicitly reports no default/fraud or term-loan misuse while noting PF, ESI and GST deposit delays (PDF66). FY2022 has the conflicting enclosure reference and responsibility disclaimer described above; its separate conclusion remains ND. A separate adequate/effective IFC opinion is present for FY2023, and FY2024–FY2026 also report effective controls. For audit trails, FY2023 says the software requirement applies from 1 April 2023; FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 affirm audit-trail software. No adverse trail qualification was located, but that wording is not proof that every historical edit log was independently tested. The Ind AS language in FY2025 audit boilerplate is not evidence of a transition when the actual policies and statements use the AS basis. [F_AR21–F_AR26; annual audit register]

The decisive unresolved matter is not an inferred allegation: original FY26 borrowing notes explicitly describe certain receivables/inventories offered as security to more than one lender and the resulting multiple financing, with management reconciling and regularizing allocation. Quarterly bank-statement differences require examination alongside this note. The fair counterweight is the audit's unmodified opinion, effective IFC conclusion and no reported default, not an assumption that the note is immaterial. Resolution requires lender-wise assets, priority/security documentation, acknowledged drawing-power reconciliation and the resulting borrowing/cash positions. [E03, E04]

The rating chronology must be read in order: BBB-/Stable/A3 in September 2025; BBB-(INC)/Negative/A3(INC) communicated September 10, 2026; then withdrawal at the company's request after lender NOC. The company did not request the adverse revision itself. Withdrawal is not proof of repayment, restored Stable outlook or a new live rating. Conversely, noncooperation is not itself a payment default. [E08]

| Original date | Statement / target | Observed outcome | Assessment / sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-11-12 | FY26 revenue growth 35–40%/40% plus | FY26 reported 27.11% growth | Miss versus headline growth guidance; different formulations preserved. [call_nov25, ar26] |
| 2025-11-12 | H2 FY26 revenue ₹260–300 cr | H2 FY26 approximately ₹308 cr | Beat the stated H2 range; do not imply every FY26 target missed. [call_nov25, ar26] |
| 2025-11-12 | PAT margin 8.5–9% | FY26 owners PAT margin approximately 7.06% | Miss on owners basis; distinguish total group PAT including NCI. [call_nov25, ar26] |
| 2025-11-12 | 100+ milk-cooler rollouts in FY26 | May 2026 call still describes successful proof-of-concept and expected H2 FY27 orders; delivered count ND | Delivery unverified, not assert zero. Timing effectively remains dependent on order intake. [call_nov25, call_may26] |
| 2026-05-18 | At least 30% growth over next 3 years and at least 12% EBITDA margin | No H1 FY27 financial results in retrieved disclosures by Oct 20 | Open forward guidance, not earned revenue. [call_may26] |
| 2026-05-18 | Positive CFO in H2 FY27/Q3–Q4 after big-project collections | Not yet measurable at cutoff | Conditional guidance, not basis to treat receivables as cash. [call_may26] |
| 2026-05-18 | ₹100 cr working-capital debt repaid in the first week of April; ₹125 cr IREDA draw occurred Q4 FY26 | Management statement; FY26 yearend debt already includes IREDA draw | Do not add ₹125 cr again to forecast opening debt, and do not infer sustainable liquidity from claimed repayment. [call_may26] |
| 2026-10-19 | 1.8 GWh BES Sfacility within 12 months | Board approval only | Track by Oct 2027, funding/commissioning/orders tests required. [bess_oct19] |

The IPO funded the company; bonus shares merely changed the denominator and did not bring new funds. Current issued, weighted-average EPS and potential hypothetical forecast shares are kept distinct. Withdrawn preferential proposals are not outstanding warrants. Related-party loans, transactions, remuneration and group balances are evaluated relative to profit, equity and cash, not presumed abusive just because they are related. [E02, E05, E06]

### History And Scope

The historical series is sourced from six original annual-report packets, FY2021 through FY2026, together with the July 2024 IPO-restated financial information. Original numbers and later comparative regroupings are retained separately. The company uses Indian GAAP/Accounting Standards, including AS 3 cash flows and AS 21 consolidation; an Ind AS reference in FY2025 auditor boilerplate is inconsistent with the accounting-policy basis and is not treated as a transition. [F_AR21–F_AR26; F_IPO pp2–9,23–25,46]

Revenue increased from ₹61.9336 crore in the FY2021 IPO-restated series to ₹419.1935 crore in FY2026. This is substantial reported scaling, but not a verified organic five-year CAGR: VEIPL was acquired in July 2020, ceased to be a subsidiary in August 2021 and was reacquired at 80% in December 2022; Powertronics was also added at 80% in December 2022. FY2022 closing assets are standalone although the restated profit statement includes the eligible part-year subsidiary period. The IPO accountant explicitly says composition and holding periods differ across years. [F_IPO pp25,46]

FY2026 operating EBITDA, excluding other income, was ₹51.7796 crore and operating EBIT ₹50.2705 crore. Group PAT was ₹30.3211 crore, of which ₹29.5727 crore belonged to owners. Finance cost rose from ₹4.1273 crore to ₹11.1066 crore. A ₹3.3005 crore deferred-tax credit partly offsets ₹13.9875 crore current tax; the deferred-tax asset includes ₹2.6826 crore for MSME disallowance. These may be legitimate timing benefits, not automatically one-offs or fictitious profit, but realization depends on payments and future taxable profits. [F_AR26 pp151,170,178–180]

### Cash Conversion

Across the three original audited FY2024–FY2026 accounts, cumulative CFO was −₹159.8230 crore against group PAT of ₹71.6932 crore: CFO/PAT is −2.2293x, calculated as a ratio of sums. Cash capex of ₹31.0445 crore takes the reported FCF proxy to −₹190.8675 crore. This cannot be explained principally by a new factory: receivables and other operating balances absorbed cash before capex. The profitable P&L and available lender finance are counterevidence to immediate insolvency, but they do not establish self-funded growth. [F_AR24 PDF85; F_AR25 PDF147; F_AR26 pp153–154]

The statements begin from parent-attributable earnings or PBT less NCI, while putting the entire NCI equity movement into financing. Reclassifying FY2024–FY2026 minority profit of ₹1.4242 crore from financing to operating increases group CFO to −₹158.3988 crore, or −2.2094x PAT, without changing total cash. After the reported financing-cost cash payments of ₹17.7334 crore, operating cash is −₹176.1322 crore, or −2.4567x PAT. Neither correction rescues cash conversion. Interest classification is therefore shown rather than treating reported CFO as cash available to owners. [F_AR24 PDF84–85; F_AR25 PDF146–147; F_AR26 pp151,153–154]

The blank FY2026 separate cash-tax line is not evidence that no tax was paid or that tax was necessarily omitted. The −₹5.7402 crore short-provision adjustment equals the ₹8.2942 crore balance-sheet increase less ₹14.0344 crore current/prior tax expense. Under a no-other-tax-movement assumption, this embeds ₹6.6166 crore of cash tax. This is a reproducible analytical explanation, not an independently disclosed paid-tax figure; subtracting it again would double-count tax. [F_AR26 pp153,167,180]

Earlier cash-flow comparability is weaker. Original FY2021, FY2022 and FY2023 CFO was ₹1.3200 crore, −₹1.1149 crore and ₹5.1886 crore respectively, versus IPO-restated ₹4.0280 crore, −₹1.6650 crore and ₹9.5513 crore. Original statements included borrowing movements in operating cash; FY2023 expressly used tax provisions instead of payments. The full consolidated regrouping bridge was not supplied separately in the IPO records. Both versions are preserved, and a cleaner five-year ratio is not invented. [F_AR21 PDF69; F_AR22 PDF34; F_AR23 PDF120–121; F_IPO pp9,46]

### Working Capital And Funding

At March 2026, trade receivables were ₹322.5253 crore and the latest-classification non-current retention balance ₹53.1199 crore, totalling ₹375.6452 crore versus ₹224.7678 crore at March 2025. The latter classification combines items previously disclosed separately, including deferred TDS, so not all retention should be assumed contractually identical or immediately collectible. Trade receivables older than one year rose from ₹18.4322 crore to ₹43.8772 crore, or 13.60% of the total. Most balances remained under six months and were classified good, which is relevant counterevidence; it is not independent collection evidence. [F_AR25 PDF157; F_AR26 pp171–174]

The creditor warning is material: ₹64.3356 crore of ₹71.3312 crore MSME payables is more than one year past the due date, not merely more than one year after invoice. The schedule states ₹61.6322 crore at one to two years, ₹2.4528 crore at two to three years and ₹0.2506 crore above three years; all are shown as undisputed. Overall payables fell from ₹121.2173 crore to ₹118.3868 crore, so FY2026 CFO was not supported by a fresh increase in total supplier credit. Back-to-back collection-linked arrangements may explain timing, but do not erase overdue supplier exposure or justify assuming indefinite rollover. [F_AR26 pp165–166]

Reported cash of ₹10.4078 crore includes term deposits. Current accounts, cash and prepaid cards total ₹6.9477 crore; deposits under three months, three to twelve months and over twelve months total another ₹12.9116 crore. Borrowing notes identify FD margins and escrow/TRA/DSRA charges but do not quantify the restricted portion. Even ₹6.9477 crore is only a provisional demand-cash modelling proxy, not certified freely available cash. Gross debt was ₹175.5303 crore, including ₹96.6719 crore current maturities. A subsequent management repayment claim cannot be inserted as a second cash inflow or accepted as audited closing liquidity. [F_AR26 pp108–111,164–165,173–174]

Other claims include ₹12.1441 crore current tax, ₹3.3359 crore statutory dues, ₹0.1075 crore accrued interest, ₹0.0107 crore unpaid dividend and ₹4.0900 crore total warranty provisions. Performance guarantees were ₹44.3667 crore; claims not acknowledged as debt ₹0.0115 crore and export-obligation customs exposure ₹1.0839 crore. The parent also disclosed ₹5.10 crore of guarantees to subsidiaries. Guarantees are stressed separately, not automatically added to funded debt or double-counted with facilities already consolidated. [F_AR26 pp85,166–167,181–182]

Debt timing remains unresolved. The standalone borrowing note attributes ₹96.5567 crore current maturities to HDFC and Yes Bank; the consolidated schedule reports ₹96.6719 crore and refers generically to bank term loans. Neither maps the later management-described ₹100 crore IREDA repayment to those maturities. Full overlap cannot be treated as verified. A model must test no, partial and full overlap, cap aggregate repayments at funded principal, and avoid treating the ₹125 crore final-quarter FY2026 draw as a new April inflow. Any assumed collections financing repayment remain a transparent analyst bridge. Clean no-default CARO reporting is counterevidence against interpreting this mapping gap as an observed default. [F_AR26 pp111,164–165; subsequent management statements require their separate source]

### Capital Returns

An exact economic ROIC remains NS because cash restrictions, government/tax asset classification and historical scope changes are unresolved. An explicit book-capital sensitivity is still informative. At March 2026, owners equity ₹138.1394 crore + NCI ₹1.8261 crore + funded debt ₹175.5303 crore + accrued interest/dividend ₹0.1182 crore, less demand/card cash ₹6.9477 crore, DTA ₹3.9545 crore, identified non-operating loans ₹1.7670 crore and interest receivable ₹0.1025 crore, gives ₹302.8423 crore of committed capital when all FDs are treated as operating collateral. Deducting all FDs gives a lower denominator of ₹289.9307 crore. Neither extreme is asserted to be the uniquely correct classification. [F_AR26 pp149–150,165–174]

At an explicitly assumed 25.17% normalized operating tax rate, FY2026 NOPAT is ₹37.6174 crore. Average-capital ROIC is about 16.14–17.07% across the FD treatments. The FY2023–FY2026 incremental proxy is ΔNOPAT ₹30.0695 crore / ΔIC ₹263.3093–274.3883 crore, or about 10.96–11.42%; FY2021–FY2026 is about 13.02–13.56%. These accounting proxies do not demonstrate durable returns clearly above a 14–18% nominal-INR analyst cost-of-capital range. Lower taxes improve them modestly; delayed utilization of the plant commissioned on 1 March 2026 is meaningful counterevidence, not yet proof of future returns. [F_IPO pp7–9,17,19–20; F_AR26 pp149–154,169–174]

The three-year capital bridge reconciles ₹31.0445 crore cash capex less ₹3.9888 crore P&L depreciation to ₹27.0557 crore, against a ₹27.0483 crore increase in net PPE, intangibles and CWIP; the residual is −₹0.0074 crore. Add ₹6.1652 crore capital advances and ₹241.1748 crore of other operating-capital growth under the stated funding definition to reach ΔIC ₹274.3883 crore. The latter is a residual, not independently established acquisition-free ONWC. The five-year fixed-asset bridge has a −₹0.5436 crore acquisition/disposal/reclassification residual and cannot support an exact organic project-return claim. [F_IPO pp7–9; F_AR26 pp149–154,168–174]

### Per Share And Minority

FY2026 issued shares were 21,972,020 after a 1:1 bonus; this is not economic dilution. The economic issuance was the 2024 IPO: 2,920,000 new shares versus 8,066,010 before the offer, increasing the count by 36.20%. The IPO price was ₹180, with ₹15 discount on 24,000 employee shares; that reconciles nominal ₹52.56 crore gross proceeds to actual ₹52.524 crore. The company reported full use by March 2025, primarily working capital, after a September 2024 statement still showed ₹7.04 crore unused. Use-of-proceeds compliance is positive evidence, but deployment into receivables is not itself a satisfactory investment return. [F_PROS cover; F_IPOUTIL pp1–3; F_AR25 pp62–63, CARO; F_AR26 pp35–36,160–162]

The proposed FY2026 preferential/share-swap issue was withdrawn, and the FY2026 annual report reports no warrants, ESOPs or other such issuance. Reported EPS of ₹13.46 should be compared with FY2025 ₹27.21 divided by two, or ₹13.605, not the unadjusted number. Owners PAT rose 7.37%, but this bonus-adjusted weighted-share EPS comparison fell about 1.1% because the prior IPO shares were outstanding for only part of FY2025. [F_AR26 pp35–36,151,181]

Minority interests matter economically. The two established Indian subsidiaries are 80%-owned and produced combined PAT of about ₹4.1195 crore; their 20% outside share is partly offset by the 25% minority share of the Uganda loss. The AOC-1 allocation approximates reported minority profit of ₹0.7484 crore, 2.468% of group PAT, with a small consolidation residual. NCI book value ₹1.8261 crore is not fair value. A fixed 2.468% group residual-share assumption is only a modelling proxy: UAE, Uganda, Sunventa and other entities have different ownership and could alter the mix. [F_AR26 pp58–60,151]

Reported CFO and analytical corrections are shown side by side. FY26's cash-flow starting figure differs from P&L PBT by the NCI share; movement in minority equity is presented in financing and includes earnings. Reclassifying those amounts changes CFO versus financing, **not the underlying cash deficit**. A blank tax-paid line is not declared proof that tax was ignored: the short-provision movement can embed tax, with a derived bridge and stated limitations. FY25's comparator relabeling also requires original-versus-later presentation reconciliation. FY23 original and restated CFO differ materially, and the original discusses provision-basis tax. These are reasons to reconcile original records, not silently adopt the higher conversion series. [E01, E02, E04]

Cash capex belongs to investing cash flow. Weak CFO is explained by receivables, retention and other operating movements, not excused by the capex program. FY26's reported ₹10.4078 crore current cash/bank line includes deposits; another ₹9.4515 crore is noncurrent deposits. Provisional demand/current/prepaid cash is only ₹6.9477 crore, and even its escrow allocation needs confirmation. The model excludes all ₹12.9116 crore identified deposits from base available cash. It does not assert every deposit is legally restricted. Deferred tax assets, capital advances and related-party loans are not cash. [E04, E07]

### Opening obligations and cash-event model

The model starts from March 31, 2026 balance-sheet claims, not EBITDA alone. Its April 7 ₹100 crore receivable receipt is an explicit **analyst bridge assumption** preceding management-stated repayment of ₹100 crore IREDA debt. No audited bank inflow/date is claimed; the ₹125 crore facility drawn in the last FY26 quarter is already in opening debt and is not added again. The payment is assumed to overlap the ₹96.6719 crore current-maturity line, with no double repayment of that same principal. The standalone note names HDFC/Yes current maturities, so overlap with the IREDA repayment is specifically unresolved. Zero/half/full-overlap sensitivities pay any remaining current portion by March 2027, capped by outstanding debt. Timing and overlap are assumptions, not verified maturity facts. [E07, E14]

Opening tax ₹12.1441, statutory dues ₹3.3359, accrued interest ₹0.1075 and dividend ₹0.0107 are settled separately from new operating tax/interest. Current employee/warranty claims and a dated long-warranty settlement are retained. Remaining customer-security/employee claims ₹2.2013 are deducted once at terminal settlement. The model includes no free tax-asset offset. Future margins include ongoing warranty/service economics; those are not confused with the opening provisions. Government balances are held as committed assets without pretending their GST/income-tax split is known. [E04, E14]

The base ratios retain supplier credit, not a legal waiver of past-due creditors. Separate half/full-cure tests require immediate settlement of ₹32.1678/₹64.3356 crore of existing overdue MSME credit on 19 November 2026 and permanently reduce supplier-credit availability by the same amount. The liability is already in payables: cash leaves once through the lower payable stock, not through a duplicate debt charge. Illustrative ₹5/₹15 crore contingency stresses cover additional guarantee/penalty risk without declaring such calls actual. [E04, E14]

Every month records supplier prepayments, customer collections, remaining operating payments, front/back capex, interest, tax, collateral, opening claims, principal and financing. Cash is tested after each event against ₹1 crore. Four intra-month cycles and front-payment fractions are assumptions with sensitivity. Finance is permitted only before the first breach, from specified dates, with ₹25 crore lifetime gross new debt and ₹25 crore gross equity at ₹60 less 4% fees, additionally capped by verified authorized shares. New debt charges 14% plus 2% fees, first-month interest and dated amortization after 12 months. No approved commitment is implied. [E14]

sections.title: Bear Case & Permanent-Loss Path
sections.content_markdown:
The strongest credible failure chain is government/project collections slip → high retention and aged debtors remain → suppliers withdraw payment linkage or lenders restrict overlapping collateral → borrowing cost/available limits worsen → BESS and EPC require cash before receipts → discounted equity or asset sales impair existing owners. Capex delay then reduces growth while fixed costs and warranty commitments persist. A quoted drawdown alone is not impairment; an unfinanceable earning asset base or dilutive recapitalization can be. [E03, E04, E07–E12]

The single thesis-break variable is **collectible, unrestricted operating cash after lender and supplier claims**, not headline PAT. The strongest contrary evidence to a purely pessimistic view is actual revenue execution, profitable operating results, no auditor-reported default, management-stated early debt repayment, reported supplier linkage and sufficient conditional collection-repair paths to demonstrate that cash improvement could materially change economics. Those positives must be verified rather than dismissed. Impairment risk is High because cash/claim uncertainty and security overlap combine; this is not a quantified fraud probability. Failed scenario values are NS rather than ordinary shareholder prices. [E01–E14]

sections.title: Final Classification & Conditional Action
sections.content_markdown:
**Hold — unresolved; research priority, not eligible for a favorable investment conclusion.** The numerical matrix is not applied to an NS score as though it were a low number. The compounder designation fails the evidence/gate requirements and does not follow from a low P/E, solar demand or rapid historical group revenue growth. Price alone cannot clear financial-reliability, funding and organic-growth questions. [E01–E15]

For an existing holder this record identifies cash, funding, reliability and execution risks to investigate; it does not assert a portfolio exit count without holdings, tax and execution context. New evidence could produce scoreable factors and a new classification. The exact three scores are preserved separately; no undisclosed overall blend or invented universe rank is supplied. Pending-evidence and gate-held records belong outside numerical rankings. This issuer report does not count itself as accepted or change the project manifest.

### Sixteen final quality checks

1. Correct legal company, ISIN, current shares, consolidated/owner scope and explicit market/information dates checked.
2. Material primary records read; V/C/M/A distinctions preserved rather than trusting search snippets or treating forecasts as facts.
3. Original audits, CARO/IFC, audit trail, RPTs, financing and dilution reviewed with fair adverse and favorable evidence.
4. Comparable periods/units kept; restatement and original differences retained; no invented TTM or quarterly cash flow.
5. Reported revenue separated from acquisitions/perimeter, price/volume uncertainty, profits and announced capacity; unsupported organic score remains NS.
6. CFO/PAT uses ratio of sums and matched group perimeter; analytical NCI/tax sensitivity separate; capex is not blamed for CFO.
7. Incremental-return numerator, denominator, timing, committed capital and limitations visible; no project IRR claimed from a distorted ratio.
8. Normalization, accounting basis, financing interest/tax, deposits, NCI, senior claims and per-share dilution are consistent and qualified.
9. Monthly/intraperiod scenario cash, capex, debt/equity fees, terminal reinvestment and reserves reconcile; failed trials retained; ordinary returns suppressed after breach.
10. Thirteen canonical factors assigned once; each score's original weights total 100%; BQS enters IAS once.
11. Missing evidence remains NS; original weight coverage, mathematical bounds and weakest material confidence shown.
12. Raw/final scores reconcile with exact Decimal; only disclosed caps applied and caps never replace NS.
13. Classification follows gate/evidence rules and complete matrix; no unsupported compounder label.
14. Official dated 60/20-session actual turnover, zero-day treatment, share/lot constraints and ₹5 lakh implementation sensitivity checked; no guaranteed fill claimed.
15. Strongest bear case, positive counterevidence and collectible-cash thesis-break variable stated.
16. Common v3.0 cutoff/tie policy retained; no fabricated batch ranking/count; substantive and portable recovery verification remain separate from source certainty.
